title: Editing Text with sed
summary: Substitute text with sed, print or delete lines by number or pattern, and edit config files in place without losing the original.
intro: `sed` is a stream editor: it reads lines, edits them with the commands you give it, and prints the result. Scripts use it to change config files, rewrite paths and URLs, and clean up text without opening an editor. In this lesson you substitute text, pick lines by number or pattern, and edit files in place. Your scripts run next to `app.conf`, `nginx.conf`, `links.txt`, and `dates.txt`.

steps.title: Substitute text
steps.body:
`s/old/new/` replaces the first match of `old` on each line with `new`. `old` is a regular expression, just like a grep pattern. Flags after the last slash change what gets replaced:

- `g` replaces every match on the line.
- A number like `2` replaces only the 2nd match.
- `I` ignores case.

```bash
echo "one two one two" | sed 's/one/1/g'
echo "one two one two" | sed 's/one/1/2'
echo "Error ERROR error" | sed 's/error/warn/Ig'
```

Any character after the `s` can be the delimiter, so `s|/var/www|/srv|` needs no backslashes before its slashes. In `new`, `&` stands for the whole match. With `-E`, parentheses capture parts of the match, and `\1`, `\2` put them back.

To run several commands, give each one its own `-e`, or separate them with `;` in one script:

```bash
echo "cat dog" | sed -e 's/cat/lion/' -e 's/dog/wolf/'
echo "cat dog" | sed 's/cat/lion/; s/dog/wolf/'
```

sed prints every line, changed or not, and the file itself stays as it was.

examples.title: First match or every match
examples.prompt: Switch the links in `links.txt` from `http:` to `https:`, first without the `g` flag, then with it.
examples.code:
echo "first match on each line:"
sed 's/http:/https:/' links.txt
echo "every match:"
sed 's/http:/https:/g' links.txt
examples.output:
first match on each line:
https://shop.example/products
https://shop.example/cart moved to http://shop.example/basket
https://docs.example/api
https://status.example
https://cdn.example/app.js http://cdn.example/app.css
every match:
https://shop.example/products
https://shop.example/cart moved to https://shop.example/basket
https://docs.example/api
https://status.example
https://cdn.example/app.js https://cdn.example/app.css
examples.explanation: Without `g`, sed replaces only the first `http:` on each line, so the two lines with two links keep their second `http:`. With `g`, every link changes. The `https:` line stays as it was, because the pattern needs a colon right after `http`. sed prints all 5 lines both times, matched or not.

examples.title: Paths and the whole match
examples.prompt: Move the site from `/var/www` to `/srv/app` in `nginx.conf`, then mark every number in `dates.txt`.
examples.code:
sed 's|/var/www|/srv/app|g' nginx.conf | grep srv
echo "numbers marked:"
sed -E 's/[0-9]+/<&>/g' dates.txt
examples.output:
root /srv/app/shop/public;
    # moved from /srv/app/old to /srv/app/shop in 2026
        alias /srv/app/shop/static/;
numbers marked:
<2026>-<10>-<03> checkout outage
<2026>-<09>-<28> release <2>.<13>.<0>
<2026>-<10>-<16> release <2>.<14>.<0>
billing period <2026>-<09>-<01> to <2026>-<09>-<30>
<2026>-<10>-<12> office closed
examples.explanation: The paths are full of slashes, and with `/` as the delimiter the command would be `s/\/var\/www/\/srv\/app/g`. With `|` it reads like the paths themselves. `grep srv` keeps just the lines that changed, and the comment line changed twice, thanks to `g`. In the second command `&` is whatever `[0-9]+` matched, so each run of digits comes back wrapped in `<` and `>`, the version numbers too.

examples.title: Capture groups
examples.prompt: Rewrite the dates in `dates.txt` from `2026-10-03` to `03/10/2026`.
examples.output:
03/10/2026 checkout outage
28/09/2026 release 2.13.0
16/10/2026 release 2.14.0
billing period 01/09/2026 to 2026-09-30
12/10/2026 office closed
every date on the line:
billing period 01/09/2026 to 30/09/2026
examples.explanation: Each pair of parentheses captures part of the match: `\1` is the year, `\2` the month, and `\3` the day, and the replacement puts them back in a new order. The replacement has slashes in it, so `|` is the delimiter again. Without `g`, only the first date on each line changes, and the billing line keeps `2026-09-30`. With `g`, both of its dates change.

practice.title: Point at the new database
practice.prompt:
Print `app.conf` with the database moved and debugging turned off.

1. Replace every `db.internal` with `db.prod.example`, the second one on a line too.
2. Replace `debug=true` with `debug=false`.
3. Leave every other line as it is.

```text
# owner: ops team

env=staging
port=8080
debug=false

# database
db_host=db.prod.example
db_replicas = db.prod.example:5433,db.prod.example:5434
#max_connections=100
timeout = 30
```

hints: You need two `s` commands. Give each one its own `-e`.
Without the `g` flag, only the first `db.internal` on a line changes.
`sed -e 's/db\.internal/db.prod.example/g' -e 's/debug=true/debug=false/' app.conf`. The backslash makes the dot match only a dot.

steps.title: Print and delete lines
steps.body:
An *address* in front of a command picks the lines it runs on. Without one, a command runs on every line.

- A number like `3` is that line, and `$` is the last line.
- `2,5` is the range from line 2 to line 5.
- `/re/` is every line that matches a regular expression.
- `/start/,/end/` runs from a line that matches `start` to the next line that matches `end`.

The commands: `p` prints the line, `d` deletes it, `i text` inserts a line before it, and `a text` appends one after it. sed prints every line anyway, so `p` alone would print lines twice. Add `-n` to turn that off, and only what `p` prints comes out:

```bash
sed '3p' fruits.txt | head -n 4
sed -n '3p' fruits.txt
sed '2,11d' fruits.txt
sed '$a # end of list' fruits.txt | tail -n 2
```

So `sed -n '/re/p'` works like grep, and `sed '1d'` like `tail -n +2`.

examples.title: Print a range
examples.prompt: Print lines 2 to 4 of `app.conf`, its last line, and its port line.
examples.code:
sed -n '2,4p' app.conf
echo "last line:"
sed -n '$p' app.conf
echo "the port line:"
sed -n '/^port=/p' app.conf
examples.output:
# owner: ops team

name = shopfront
last line:
timeout = 30
the port line:
port=8080
examples.explanation: `-n` turns off sed's own printing, so only the lines that `p` prints appear. `2,4p` prints lines 2, 3, and 4, and line 3 is blank, so it prints as an empty line. `$` is the last line, however long the file is. `/^port=/p` prints the lines that start with `port=`, just like `grep '^port='`.

examples.title: Delete noise
examples.prompt: Print `app.conf` without its comment lines, then without comments and blank lines.
examples.output:
name = shopfront
env=staging
port=8080
debug=true

db_host=db.internal
db_replicas = db.internal:5433,db.internal:5434
timeout = 30
---
name = shopfront
env=staging
port=8080
debug=true
db_host=db.internal
db_replicas = db.internal:5433,db.internal:5434
timeout = 30
examples.explanation: `/^#/d` deletes every line that starts with `#`, including `#max_connections=100`, a setting someone commented out. The blank lines stay, which is why the first output starts with one. A second command, `/^$/d`, deletes the lines with nothing between their start and their end. sed runs both commands on each line in turn, and a deleted line goes no further.

examples.title: Blocks and inserts
examples.prompt: Print the `server` block of `nginx.conf`, drop the header of `employees.csv`, and add a first line to `app.conf`.
examples.code:
sed -n '/^server {/,/^}/p' nginx.conf
echo "no header:"
sed '1d' employees.csv | head -n 2
echo "with a first line:"
sed '1i # generated by deploy.sh' app.conf | head -n 2
examples.explanation: The range starts at the line that begins with `server {` and ends at the next line that begins with `}`. The `location` blocks inside are indented, so their closing braces don't end the range early, and the indented `server` line in the `upstream` block doesn't start it. `1d` deletes line 1, the header. `1i` inserts a new line before line 1, and sed prints it like any other.

practice.title: Clean config
practice.prompt:
Print a clean copy of `app.conf`, the way a script would read it.

1. Delete the comment lines, the ones that start with `#`.
2. Delete the blank lines.
3. Remove the spaces around `=`, so `name = shopfront` becomes `name=shopfront`.

Expected output:

```text
name=shopfront
env=staging
port=8080
debug=true
db_host=db.internal
db_replicas=db.internal:5433,db.internal:5434
timeout=30
```

hints: Start from the delete-noise example, then add an `s` command.
Give each command its own `-e`: two `d` commands and one `s` command.
`s/ *= */=/` replaces an `=` and any spaces around it with a bare `=`.

steps.title: Edit files in place
steps.body:
So far sed has printed its result and left the file alone. `-i` edits the file in place instead: sed saves the result back into the file and prints nothing. That's handy and risky, so keep a backup:

- `sed -i 's/a/b/' file` changes `file` and keeps no copy.
- `sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' file` saves the original as `file.bak` first.

```bash
sed -i.bak 's/^debug=true/debug=false/' app.conf
grep '^debug=' app.conf app.conf.bak
```

On macOS, sed wants the suffix as its own argument, so there you write `sed -i '' 's/a/b/' file` for no backup. `-i.bak` works the same on both.

A common job is to *upsert* a setting: replace its line when the key exists, and append one when it doesn't. grep's exit status makes the choice:

```bash
grep -q '^env=' app.conf && sed -i 's/^env=.*/env=production/' app.conf || echo 'env=production' >> app.conf
grep '^env=' app.conf
```

examples.title: Change a setting
examples.prompt: Change the port in `app.conf` to 9090 in place, keeping a backup, then run `sed -i.bak` on a file where nothing matches.
examples.code:
sed -i.bak 's/^port=.*/port=9090/' app.conf
grep '^port=' app.conf app.conf.bak
echo "config.ini has no workers line:"
sed -i.bak 's/^workers=.*/workers=4/' config.ini
ls *.bak
examples.output:
app.conf:port=9090
app.conf.bak:port=8080
config.ini has no workers line:
app.conf.bak
config.ini.bak
examples.explanation: `-i.bak` copies the original to `app.conf.bak`, then saves the change into `app.conf`, and prints nothing while it does. `^port=.*` matches the whole port line: `.*` runs to the end of the line, so the old value goes however long it was. With two files, grep starts each match with the file's name, which puts the new port next to the old one. `config.ini` has no `workers=` line, so nothing in it changes, but `-i.bak` still writes `config.ini.bak`: every run makes a backup, match or not.

examples.title: Uncomment a line
examples.prompt: Turn the commented-out `max_connections` setting back on.
examples.code:
grep max_connections app.conf
sed -i -E 's/^#(max_connections)/\1/' app.conf
grep max_connections app.conf
examples.explanation: The group captures `max_connections`, and the replacement writes it back without the `#` in front. The `^` makes sure only a line that *starts* with `#max_connections` changes, not a comment that mentions the setting later in a sentence. Plain `-i` keeps no backup, so use it when the change is small and easy to undo.

examples.title: Upsert a setting
examples.prompt: Set `workers` in `app.conf`, which has no such line yet, then set it again to a new value.
examples.code:
grep -q '^workers=' app.conf && sed -i 's/^workers=.*/workers=4/' app.conf || echo 'workers=4' >> app.conf
tail -n 1 app.conf
grep -q '^workers=' app.conf && sed -i 's/^workers=.*/workers=8/' app.conf || echo 'workers=8' >> app.conf
tail -n 2 app.conf
examples.explanation: The first time, `app.conf` has no `workers=` line, so `grep -q` exits 1, `&&` skips the `sed`, and `||` appends the line. The second time grep finds it, `sed -i` rewrites it to `workers=8`, and since `sed` succeeds, the `echo` after `||` is skipped. The file ends with one `workers` line either way, so the script is safe to run again and again.

practice.title: Set the port
practice.prompt:
Set the port in `app.conf` to 8081, keeping a backup, whether or not the file has a port line yet.

1. Replace the `port=` line in place with `sed -i.bak`, which also saves the original as `app.conf.bak`.
2. If `app.conf` still has no `port=` line, append `port=8081`.
3. Print `app.conf`.

Check also runs your script on an `app.conf` without a port line, and `app.conf.bak` must be there too.

Expected output:

```text
# shopfront app settings
# owner: ops team

name = shopfront
env=staging
port=8081
debug=true

# database
db_host=db.internal
db_replicas = db.internal:5433,db.internal:5434
#max_connections=100
timeout = 30
```

hints: `sed -i.bak` writes the backup even when no line matches, like `config.ini.bak` in the examples. So run it first, every time.
After the `sed`, `grep -q '^port=' app.conf` tells you whether a port line exists.
`grep -q '^port=' app.conf || echo 'port=8081' >> app.conf` appends the line only when grep finds none.

recap:
- `sed 's/old/new/' file` replaces the first match on each line. `g` replaces every match, `2` only the second, and `I` ignores case.
- Pick another delimiter for paths: `s|/var/www|/srv|`. `&` is the whole match, and `-E` groups come back as `\1`, `\2`.
- Addresses pick lines: `3`, `2,5`, `$`, `/re/`, and `/start/,/end/`. `-n` with `p` prints only those lines, `d` deletes them, and `1i` and `$a` add lines.
- Run several commands with `-e cmd -e cmd`, or `cmd; cmd` in one script.
- `-i.bak` edits a file in place and keeps the original. On macOS, write `sed -i ''` for no backup.
- Upsert: `grep -q '^key=' f && sed -i 's/^key=.*/key=v/' f || echo 'key=v' >> f`.
